summaries.example: Imagine a school play. Students have different roles: actors perform, stage crew moves objects, and a director helps organize everyone. Rules explain what each role does. The play works because people coordinate their actions. A school is more lasting and complex than one play, but the example shows how roles, rules, shared work, and goals can fit together.
summaries.summary: A social institution is a lasting and organized part of social life. Examples include schools, hospitals, governments, families, businesses, languages, and legal systems. Institutions are made from connected roles and rules. The people in those roles depend on one another, and their work may serve a purpose such as teaching, healing, governing, or producing goods. Institutions also have informal cultures: shared attitudes and habits that may not be written down. They can use informal sanctions, such as disapproval, or formal sanctions, such as official punishment. Philosophers offer different explanations. Some focus on individuals coordinating their actions. Others focus on shared acceptance, common goals, rules, or the larger structure of society. The entry also asks whether an institution can think and act as a group, or whether only its members are agents. Institutions guide and enable people, but people can also change them.
key_ideas: Social institutions are complex and usually last across many generations.
Institutions include roles, rules, relationships, goals, and often shared ways of doing things.
Schools, hospitals, businesses, governments, families, languages, and legal systems can be institutions.
Philosophers disagree about whether institutions are mainly collections of individual actions, larger systems, or structured units of their own.
Institutions can help people cooperate, but they can also involve power, limits, unfairness, and penalties.
People shape institutions, while institutions also influence what people can do and how they behave.
summaries.why_it_matters: Institutions affect everyday life. They decide who has certain jobs, powers, responsibilities, and benefits. Understanding them helps us ask whether their rules work well, whether their goals are being met, and whether people are treated fairly. It also helps explain why changing an institution can be difficult: many roles, habits, expectations, and relationships are connected.

important_terms.definition: A lasting, organized way that people work together, such as a school, hospital, government, or language.
A job or place in an organized group, with tasks and rules connected to it.
A guide that says what people may, must, or should do.
The way people’s actions fit together so they can achieve something or avoid a problem.
An aim or purpose that an institution’s activities may help achieve.

questions_to_think_about: What makes a school more than just a group of people in one building?
Which rules in an institution help people cooperate?
Can an institution be useful in some ways and unfair in others?
How much freedom do people have inside an institution?

summaries.example: Consider a university admissions system. It contains roles—applicants, instructors, admissions officers, and administrators—along with rules about applications, evaluation, and decisions. Its procedures coordinate many people who do not know one another. Yet the system also has a culture, such as assumptions about merit, and power relations that affect whose judgments count. One philosophical question is whether the university is reducible to the actions and attitudes of its members, or whether its structured rules and offices give it a distinct kind of unity.
summaries.summary: The entry examines what social institutions are and how they operate. In its main usage, an institution is a complex, enduring social form—often an organization or system of organizations—such as a government, university, hospital, corporation, legal system, family, or language. It has a structure of differentiated, interdependent roles; formal and informal rules; a culture of attitudes and practices; functions or ends; power relations; and sometimes sanctions. Institutions are not simply identical with isolated conventions or rules, nor are they necessarily parts that can be understood only through the entire society. The entry compares several theories. Atomistic and rational-choice accounts begin with individuals and explain institutions through coordinated behavior, incentives, expectations, and rules. Collective-acceptance accounts hold that institutions depend on shared attitudes, including views about status roles and institutional facts. The teleological account explains organizations through joint actions directed toward collective ends, especially collective goods that can ground moral rights and duties. Bratman’s procedural model emphasizes shared plans, social rules, and higher-level rules that organize roles and authority in large institutions. A final debate concerns agency: some theorists argue that institutions can reason and act as collective agents, while others analyze institutional action through members, procedures, and external conditions. Institutions shape individual action but do not completely determine it; people interpret, revise, resist, and reproduce institutional structures.
key_ideas: The entry uses a sociological sense of institution: complex social forms that reproduce themselves, including organizations and systems of organizations.
Institutions should be distinguished from simpler forms such as rules, norms, conventions, roles, and rituals, and from more comprehensive entities such as societies and cultures.
Important dimensions include structure, function, culture, power, and sanctions. Structure connects differentiated and often hierarchical roles whose tasks may be interdependent.

Rational-choice approaches explain institutions through coordination, incentives, expectations, and rules in equilibrium. Critics argue that coordination alone may not explain institutional unity, purpose, or moral features.
Collective-acceptance theories emphasize shared attitudes and sometimes constitutive rules, while teleological theories emphasize joint action, collective ends, and collective goods.

A procedural social-rule model explains large organizations through interconnected rules about rules, including rules that establish offices and authority. The entry also examines whether institutions themselves are agents and how structure relates to individual agency.
summaries.why_it_matters: Institutions distribute benefits, burdens, authority, opportunities, and responsibilities. They are therefore central to questions about justice, political organization, social power, and individual autonomy. A theory of justice needs some account of the institutions to which its principles apply. Studying institutions also clarifies why formal rules may differ from institutional culture, why organizations can outlast their members, and why institutional change may result from both intentional design and unintended consequences.

important_terms.definition: A complex, relatively enduring social form made up of connected roles, practices, norms, values, and often organizations.
An account that explains institutions through individual actions and their interdependence, often using incentives and expectations.
An account that emphasizes how institutions depend on their relations to one another and their contribution to wider social systems.
An account that treats an institution as having structured elements and unity without reducing it either to simple rules or to the whole society.
A stable pattern of action that solves a coordination problem because people expect others to act similarly.
A shared or group-directed attitude involved in acting together; theorists disagree about whether it reduces to individual attitudes.
An institution’s purpose or contribution, such as education for a university or health care for a hospital.
The capacity to affect what others can do, often through roles, authority, incentives, or constraints.

questions_to_think_about: Does a bundle of conventions become an institution merely by being connected, or must it have a deeper structure and purpose?
Are institutional rights and duties created by collective acceptance, grounded in moral needs, or both?
Can an organization have intentions of its own, or are apparent institutional intentions reducible to members’ actions and procedures?
How can institutions constrain individuals while also enabling actions they could not perform alone?
When an institution reproduces itself, is this usually the result of deliberate purpose, unintended consequences, or a mixture?

summaries.example: Think about a student council deciding how to spend money for school activities. There are roles, such as chairperson, treasurer, and representatives, plus rules for proposing and voting on ideas. Students coordinate because they expect others to follow the procedure. The council also develops a culture: perhaps members listen carefully, or perhaps older students usually control discussions even when the written rules do not say so. This shows why an institution includes more than a list of rules.
summaries.summary: Social institutions are complex and relatively lasting ways of organizing social life. They include schools, governments, hospitals, families, corporations, languages, and legal systems. An institution commonly has connected roles, rules, tasks, authority relationships, informal culture, and a purpose or function. It is more complex than a single convention, norm, ritual, or role, yet less complete than an entire society. Many institutions are organizations, and some—especially governments—organize other institutions. The entry compares competing explanations. Individualist theories begin with people and their interdependent choices. Rational-choice approaches emphasize coordination problems, expectations, incentives, and rules that people have reason to follow. Holistic theories stress how institutions fit into larger social systems. Other accounts treat each institution as a structured unit with its own elements and unity. Collective-acceptance theories say institutions depend on shared acceptance, especially when objects or people receive institutional statuses and related rights and duties. The teleological account explains institutions through joint action aimed at collective ends and sometimes collective goods. A procedural model focuses on webs of rules, including rules that establish offices and authority. The entry also explores whether institutions can be agents and how institutional structure both limits and enables individual action.
key_ideas: Institutions include governments, schools, hospitals, families, businesses, languages, and legal systems, but they are not the same as simple rules or as whole societies.
Their structure connects different roles. What one role does may depend on what other roles do, and roles can be arranged by status or authority.
Written rules do not tell the whole story. Institutional culture can shape behavior through informal expectations and attitudes.
Some theories explain institutions from the actions of individuals and coordination problems. Others begin with the larger social system or with an institution’s own structure and purpose.
Collective-acceptance theories stress shared attitudes and rules that can give people new statuses, rights, and duties. Teleological theories instead stress joint action and shared ends or goods.
Institutions influence people, but people also interpret rules, use discretion, and sometimes change or challenge institutions.
summaries.why_it_matters: Institutions organize major parts of life and help determine who receives services, makes decisions, carries responsibilities, or faces penalties. They can support cooperation and meet needs, but they can also carry power relationships and unfair practices. Understanding their structure and purposes gives us better tools for judging institutions and thinking about how they might be changed.

important_terms.definition: A lasting, complex social arrangement, often an organization or system of organizations, that organizes important human activities.
A connected set of jobs or positions, each with tasks and responsibilities.
An accepted pattern of behavior that helps people coordinate when they depend on one another.
The informal attitudes, values, habits, and “spirit” that influence how an institution actually works.
A theory that starts with individuals and explains larger social arrangements through their actions, expectations, and cooperation.
A theory that emphasizes how institutions form a connected social system and support the stability or activity of that system.
A theory saying that institutions are created or maintained through what people collectively accept or treat as true.
An institution’s goal or contribution, such as teaching in a school or healing in a hospital.

questions_to_think_about: Why is a school more than a collection of rules such as “arrive on time” and “complete your work”?
Can people follow an institution’s rules without sharing its goals?
Should an institution’s informal culture count as part of what the institution is?
Do institutions mostly solve coordination problems, or do they also create power and responsibility?
When people say “the council decided,” who or what actually made the decision?
